The present study is a pre-registered replication of a study by Specker et al. (2018) that tests the
hypothesis that brightness of colors is associated with positivity.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding identify Specker et al. (2018), 'The universal and automatic association between brightness and positivity' (Acta Psychologica, 186, 47-53, DOI: 10.1016/j.actpsy.2018.04.007) as the single original paper directly re-tested across Studies 1 and 2 (lines 14-15, 71-73, 471-476). Other cited works (e.g., Hemphill, 1996; Lakens et al., 2012, 2013; Schietecat et al., 2018) are discussed only as background context.

decisions.location: Abstract, p. 1, lines 14-22 (and Introduction, p. 2, lines 80-85; Study 1 Method & Discussion, pp. 2-3, lines 115-117, 161-164; Study 2 Discussion, p. 5, lines 280-283; Figure 3, p. 6, lines 302-322)
decisions.quote:
The present study is a pre-registered replication of a study by Specker et al. (2018) that tests the
hypothesis that brightness of colors is associated with positivity. Our results showed an implicit association
between brightness and positivity in both Study 1 and Study 2, however, an explicit association between
brightness and positivity was only found in Study 2, thereby replicating 3 out of 4 effects. To investigate
these effects in more detail, we present a meta-analysis of both the original and the replication study.
This indicated a large effect 1.31 [1.12, 1.51]. In addition, we used meta-analysis to assess potential
moderators of the effect, in particular stimulus type (chromatic vs. achromatic) and measure type (implicit
vs. explicit). This indicated that the effect is stronger when measured implicitly than when measured
explicitly and that the effect is stronger when achromatic stimuli are used. In sum, we take these findings
to indicate that there is a strong and replicable association between brightness and positivity.
decisions.reason: Both shipped row 936 and blind target 0 coded 'mixed' based on the phrase 'replicating 3 out of 4 effects', but a full reading of the primary source shows that all three empirical findings actually reported in the original Specker et al. (2018, DOI: 10.1016/j.actpsy.2018.04.007) paper replicated. Specifically, the authors explicitly state that in the original Specker et al. (2018) paper, Study 1 (chromatic patches) included only an implicit IAT measure, whereas Study 2 (achromatic patches) included both an implicit IAT measure and an explicit rating task ('In the original study only Study 2 included an explicit measure, for our replication we also included this measure in Study 1', Introduction, p. 2, lines 80-83; 'Our method, materials and procedure was identical to Study 1 of Specker et al. (2018), thus we used an IAT the only difference being that we included an explicit rating task', Study 1 Method, lines 115-117; corroborated by Figure 3, lines 302-322, which plots only Study 1 Original Implicit, Study 2 Original Implicit, and Study 2 Original Explicit). Every original study result replicated with large effects: original Study 1's implicit chromatic association replicated ('Study 1 replicated the findings of Study 1 of Specker et al. (2018) meaning that both studies found a large effect for the implicit association of brightness and positivity', lines 161-164, dz = 1.73), and original Study 2's implicit (dz = 4.07) and explicit (dz = 3.06) achromatic associations both replicated ('Study 2 replicated the findings of Study 2 of Specker et al. (2018) meaning that both studies found a large effect for the implicit and explicit association of brightness and positivity', lines 280-283). Although the authors remark that 'Study 1 did not show an explicit effect for the association between brightness and positivity that should theoretically have been there, we therefore interpret this as a failure to replicate' (lines 164-167), that fourth test was a newly added extension condition in Study 1 testing a theoretical expectation rather than a comparison against an existing Study 1 finding of Specker et al. (2018). Under Codebook Step 3 (Rule 1: overall verdict governs; Rule 2a: a comparison requires an actual finding reported by the original study; and under 'mixed': 'A count of how many measures replicated is not by itself such a mark') and FIELD_REVIEW_INSTRUCTIONS.md ('Main-message hierarchy in the codebook governs outcomes: use the authors' overall verdict where supplied... New extension/control outcomes do not automatically change replication outcomes'), all original comparisons succeeded and the authors' overall conclusion ('In sum, we take these findings to indicate that there is a strong and replicable association between brightness and positivity', Abstract lines 21-22; General Discussion lines 392-393, 441-443) establishes 'successful'.
